The manufacturing sale had not been completed; AMD was actively seeking a strategic partner [S2].

Intel's FY2025 Q2 Form 10-Q (period ended 2025-06-28) states the condition for continuing Intel 14A development is securing a significant external customer for the node. The filing says: "If we are unable to secure a significant external customer for our Intel 14A node, we may pause or discontinue development of Intel 14A and subsequent next generation leading-edge nodes" [S5]. Similarly, in MD&A: "if we are unable to secure a significant external customer and meet important customer milestones for Intel 14A, we face the prospect that it will not be economical to develop and manufacture Intel 14A and successor leading-edge nodes on a go-forward basis. In such event, we may pause or discontinue our pursuit of Intel 14A and successor nodes and various of our manufacturing expansion projects" [S9].

Intel acknowledges it "has been unsuccessful to date in securing any significant external foundry customers for any of our nodes and our prospects for securing a significant external foundry customer for Intel 14A are uncertain" [S5]. Intel states it "remains focused on continued development of Intel 14A and securing such a significant external customer," but has "taken steps to reduce our overall investment and have further slowed down the construction of the new leading-edge fabrication facilities we are building in Ohio" [S5].

The filing describes potential manufacturing consequences if the pause/discontinuation occurred, but does not state the plan has been executed. These include: losing eligibility for various government incentive arrangements and possibly being required to repay amounts already received [S4]; potentially accelerating a move to third-party foundry services and being unable to satisfy construction and/or wafer demand and purchase commitments under SCIP agreements (the 2022 Brookfield Arizona investment and 2024 Apollo Fab 34 Ireland investment), potentially requiring substantial additional payments to SCIP partners [S4]; and damaging external foundry prospects because existing nodes (Intel 7, 4, 3) were designed for Intel products, and potential customers for Intel 18A-P may remain with current foundry partners if they believe Intel is no longer committed to next-generation nodes [S7]. Additional risks include adverse impacts to customer, supplier, and strategic partner relationships, credit rating risk, diminished investor confidence, increased stock price volatility, and possible U.S./other government actions viewing discontinuation as a strategic national economic or defense risk [S2].

If discontinuation occurred, Intel expects a majority of its products would continue to be manufactured in its own facilities utilizing nodes up to Intel 18A-P through at least 2030 [S8]. The filing presents the scenario as conditional, not an already completed cancellation.

In its FY2025 Form 10-K (period ended January 26, 2025), NVIDIA defines an indirect customer as an entity that "purchase[s] products through our direct customers," where direct customers buy products directly from NVIDIA (such as AIBs, distributors, ODMs, OEMs, and system integrators). Indirect customers include CSPs, consumer internet companies, enterprises, and public sector entities [S4]. Thus, an NVIDIA indirect customer is a downstream buyer of NVIDIA hardware that obtains the products through a direct customer rather than directly from NVIDIA.

Qualcomm, in its FY2025 Form 10-K (period ended September 28, 2025), describes its QTL (Qualcomm Technology Licensing) business as granting licenses or otherwise providing rights to use portions of Qualcomm's intellectual property portfolio, including patent rights essential to and/or useful in the manufacture, sale and/or use of certain wireless products [S6]. QTL licensees manufacture wireless cellular products such as mobile devices, tablets, PCs, modem cards, embedded modules, connected vehicle units, and wireless access points [S10]. QTL licensing revenues consist primarily of per-unit royalties, with licensees paying quarterly royalties based on their sales of products incorporating or using Qualcomm's licensed IP [S9]. QTL is operated by QUALCOMM Incorporated, which owns the vast majority of Qualcomm's patent portfolio [S7].

These labels should not be treated as the same kind of chip buyer because they refer to fundamentally different roles. An NVIDIA indirect customer is a downstream purchaser of physical NVIDIA products obtained through a distribution channel (a direct customer); the relationship is a product-sale/resale chain. A QTL licensee is a manufacturer that obtains patent rights from Qualcomm to make and sell wireless products and pays royalties based on those sales; it is not buying Qualcomm chips from an intermediary. The NVIDIA label concerns how chips are purchased (directly vs. indirectly), while the QTL label concerns who is licensed to manufacture products using Qualcomm's patented IP. One is a channel/distribution distinction over hardware; the other is a licensing/royalty relationship over intellectual property.

NVIDIA's FY2024 Form 10-K (year ended Jan 28, 2024) reports two reportable segments: Compute & Networking and Graphics [S5]. They are not defined by product type alone but by what the CODM reviews; Note 17 describes their contents [S1].

Compute & Networking includes the Data Center accelerated computing platform, networking, automotive AI Cockpit and autonomous-driving agreements, electric vehicle computing platforms, Jetson for robotics, NVIDIA AI Enterprise and other software, and DGX Cloud [S1]. Graphics includes GeForce GPUs for gaming and PCs, GeForce NOW, gaming-platform solutions, Quadro/NVIDIA RTX GPUs, virtual GPU software, automotive infotainment platforms, and Omniverse Enterprise software [S1].

Reported FY2024 revenue by reportable segment, in millions (table units "in millions"):

Compute & Networking: $47,405 [S7], also shown in the segment disclosure table [S8]
Graphics: $13,517 [S7], also shown in the segment disclosure table [S8]
Total: $60,922 [S7]

NVIDIA's MD&A explains the Compute & Networking increase was driven by higher Data Center revenue [S4].

Data Center is not a third reportable segment. NVIDIA's CODM reviews operations on two segments only [S5]. Data Center is instead a specialized market that lives inside the Compute & Networking segment — Note 17 explicitly lists the "Data Center accelerated computing platform" within Compute & Networking [S1]. The separate market table shows Data Center revenue of $47,525 million for the same fiscal year [S6], and the segment discussion attributes Compute & Networking growth to higher Data Center revenue [S4].

So the distinction is: Compute & Networking covers accelerated-computing, AI, networking, software, and automotive-computing platforms; Graphics covers gaming GPUs, GeForce NOW, professional visualization, virtual GPU, infotainment, and Omniverse. Data Center is a market within Compute & Networking rather than a standalone segment.
